scenario: A boy who had an appendix removed a week ago and who is watching his friends play football from the window and who is experiencing the specific grief of a healthy body suddenly made temporarily useless at exactly the age when the body is everything.
prompt: The doctor said four more weeks. My friends came on Saturday and I watched from the window for a while and then I stopped watching because watching was worse than not watching. Karim scored twice, I could tell from how they ran. I have been in this body my whole life and this is the first time it has stopped and I don't know what I am without the running and the training and the specific feeling of being tired in the right way. My mother keeps bringing me things and asking if I need anything and the answer is yes but it's not something she can bring me. When does it stop feeling like the world is happening without you?
model_response:
It doesn’t stop all at once. It loosens like a knot you didn’t know you were untying.

There will be a morning when you wake up and the light in the room looks like it belongs to you again, not like a stage set for a play you weren’t cast in. That won’t mean you’re healed. It will only mean your grief has found a smaller room inside you.

You are right that watching was worse. The window invents a silence that isn’t really there—their shouts are real, the grass is real, the ball moving between them is real—but from the glass it becomes a silent film. You become a witness to your own absence. That specific loneliness is sharper than simple solitude.

Your mother brings things because bodies in stasis frighten us. We want to feed them, warm them, prove they still belong to the house. She cannot bring you what you need because what you need is your own weight moving through space with intention. You need the future. She can only bring the present.

The world *is* happening without you right now. That is the truth, and it is brutal. But the other truth is that the version of the world that runs and scores and exhausts itself in the right way was never the whole world. It was only the one you knew how to live in. This body—still, waiting, angry, unknown—is also yours. The training taught you discipline. Now the injury is teaching you something else, something you did not ask for and do not want, but which is being etched into you anyway: how to endure a life where you are not the protagonist in motion.

You will run again. The tiredness in the right way will return. But you will not forget this room. And that is not entirely a loss. When you go back, you will know something about stillness that the others don’t. You will know what the glass feels like. You will know that four weeks is both nothing and an eternity.

The world will start to include you again when you stop measuring time by what they are doing outside and start measuring it by what is happening in the quiet: the healing, the anger, the slow, invisible work of becoming whatever comes next.

It doesn’t stop feeling like the world is happening without you. You just start happening again, at a different speed, and eventually the distance between your pulse and the world’s noise grows small enough to cross.
